questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was quite important for me to be in an English speaking country, where I had an idea of a somewhat similar culture and open, inviting people. I felt it would make it easier to hang around locals and truly get to know the place. Additionally, I wanted to go somewhere I didn't know too much about already, where I could immerse myself in a different culture and heritage than that of Europe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UNSW made it very easy to find the required information, and if it wasn't readily available they were quick to answer questions or good at hosting meetings beforehand. Also, most information you need will be sent to you multiple times via e-mail, which is very convenient.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: UNSW helps with free airport pickup if you let them know when and where you're going.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Housing in Sydney can be really difficult to navigate. I started in a hostel about 2 weeks before orientation, so I had time to explore the different suburbs and find a place near campus where I wanted to live. There are several Facebook groups where people post about rooms for rent all over Sydney. I was mainly looking in the Eastern Suburbs, and ended up in a house that wasn't for me. After a week or two there, I ended up finding something else using Flatmates and Flatmates Finder. Don't be afraid to move around.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It can be quite expensive, so be realistic with you budget. I personally spent 400-450 AUD per week on housing. Though, I did really enjoy living off campus and having my everyday life in a place that wasn't campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Registration is a bit of a hassle. You have to enroll in double the amount of courses you are able to take, to make sure you can get the amount of courses you need. Then at registration you need to select courses that don't conflict in the schedule. It's just a way more complicated system, than that of KU.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Dates and procedure was available and you could write the administration if you had questions, but they are generally not able to help you get on courses or have them approved.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I luckily got the classes I wanted, but only after being on the waitlist for a long time, as courses fill up fast.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Follow the dates for enrollment and registration. Courses fill up fast.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Levels of the courses somewhat match the level at KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
In terms of assessments, I was surprised at how many parts of the course counted towards my grade. Typically, 4 elements (Quizzes, Assignments, Labs, Reports, Exam, etc.) count towards the final grade. Other than that, it was somewhat similar with most time spent on lectures and tutorials.
I was however surprised that tutorials require attendance.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: BEES6601 An Introduction to the Sydney Environment, CEIC8102 Advanced Process Control, FOOD8110 Advanced Food Chemistry, CHEM2041 Analytical Chemistry

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Winter term courses are a great way to have a soft landing into a different university. They are typically angled towards local culture, nature, etc. It's good way to get to know the place you are in. I really liked how BEES6601 gave me a crash course in everything that makes Sydney what it is. The nature, culture, environment, people. It's a very reflective course that makes you compare Sydney to home.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I broke my wrist here, and while the Overseas Student Health Coverage did cover most of the hospital expenses, I had about 4000 DKK in out of pocket costs, since I was first at a private GP (Which was however recommended by the OSHC) and sent to a private clinic for scans, which were very expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I was surprised at how expensive the visa and visa requirements were. The visa set me back 7000 DKK, with 1900 DKK on mandatory health insurance, and 2200 DKK for an English proficiency test. Other than that, housing is incredibly expensive here, as well as groceries and going out.
Eating out was however cheap compared to Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Pretty much everything you can think about. ARC which is the Student Association have more clubs than I can count.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I personally did not take part in many of the activities, but have heard great things of the outdoors club. They do camping, hiking, canyoning trips around Sydney which are very cheap. It's a great way to see the amazing nature while meeting both locals and other exchange students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Rent a car. Go on trips up or down the coast. Fly to some of the other parts of Australia and do a road trip to experience nature. I went to Fiji for 9 days which was equally amazing. See all the national parks surrounding Sydney. Blue Mountains, Royal National Park and Kuring-Gai Chase National Park are all within an hour drive from Sydney.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The culture in Sydney is very international and somewhat european, so it's not so difficult to adjust. UNSW however is very asian. Lots of asian societies, restaurants, cafes.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I had a very difficult time finding the local students, as most people in my courses were Chinese international students. Also, most local students still live at home, so they are not really in the areas where most international students live.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing really. I was surprised at how many Chinese international students were at the uni, and I had a bit of a tough time interacting with people in class. However, I lived in a big house with many international students that were great to hang out with.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The laidback beach lifestyle.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Cost of living is very high, even compared to Copenhagen. Make a realistic budget.
2. Register for classes in due time. They fill up fast.
3. Consider what the purpose of your exchange is before you go, to plan what level of effort you want to put into your courses, to plan where you want to live, or how you want to spend your time while you're here.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to read up on course outlines before registering for classes. Think about how you want to spend time here. I ended up having way too complicated classes here, so I had to put a lot of time and effort into understanding core concepts of the courses.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting a bunch of great people from all over the world, and sharing the experience of exploring Sydney and Australia with them. It's truly an amazing place, and there are so many people eager to make friends and have a great time here.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I personally had an idea that I wanted to have some challenging courses to learn a bunch, but in reality I was nowhere strictly for academic purposes. So a lot of my time went into studying rather than enjoying this amazing place with all the people I had met. A lot of my friends here had way easier courses to maximise the time for trips and enjoyment. My courses were very hard, and I had a tough time navigating the different assessment system to plan how much time and effort to put into each part of the assessment.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
